title: commit-runway-optimizer-and-marginal-cost-proposal
content:
Executive summary:

This working sheet proposes a small, testable commit-sizing strategy (the "Commit Runway Optimizer") that balances committed-reserved GPU amortization against marginal cost reductions from higher utilization and preemptable mixes. Goal: produce 3 clear commit size recommendations (pilot, scale, enterprise) and a sensitivity heatmap for utilization and preemptable mix so sales and finance can sign off on a limited set of contract templates.

Background / motivation:
- Sales is seeing pushback on 12–36 month reserved commitments because buyers fear overcommit and unpredictable product growth.
- Engineering wants fewer micro-variants to operate; finance wants predictable revenue and reasonable amortization periods for GPUs.
- Current models in the folder tend to assume steady-state utilization and broad tier buckets; this doc emphasizes runway (months-to-amortize) plus marginal unit economics to make short-to-medium commitments attractive.

Key definitions in this sheet (inputs):
- commit_GPU_months: total GPU-months reserved by the customer for the term (integer)
- amortization_months: internal accounting window to attribute hardware cost (12/24/36)
- baseline_hourly_cost_hosted: our on-demand equivalent cost used to compute savings
- reserved_effective_hourly_rate: negotiated rate per GPU-hour after commit discount and amortization
- expected_utilization_percent: percent of GPU time customer uses in the reserved pool (0–100)
- preemptable_share_percent: percent of reserved capacity that's allowed to be preemptable (lower $ but higher risk)
- fallback_buffer_hours: extra capacity we keep to guarantee SLAs (in hours/month)

Model formulas (spreadsheet cell pseudocode):
- reserved_hourly_rate = (capex_equivalent_per_gpu * num_gpus / (amortization_months * 730)) * (1 - commit_discount_pct) + opex_per_hour
- effective_unit_cost_per_token = reserved_hourly_rate / (avg_tokens_per_hour)
- marginal_savings_per_gpu_hour = baseline_hourly_cost_hosted - reserved_hourly_rate * (1 - preemptable_discount_pct * preemptable_share_percent)
- break_even_utilization = reservation_cost_share / baseline_hourly_cost_hosted (illustrative cell to compute util threshold where reserved beats on-demand)

Sample input table (example values used for scenarios):
- commit_GPU_months: pilot=120, scale=600, enterprise=2400
- amortization_months: 24
- baseline_hourly_cost_hosted: $3.50 / GPU-hour
- capex_equivalent_per_gpu (inc. infra) = $70,000; opex_per_hour = $0.30; commit_discount_pct: depends on bucket (pilot 0.10, scale 0.25, enterprise 0.45)
- expected_utilization_percent: pilot 60%, scale 78%, enterprise 92% (baseline assumptions)
- preemptable_share_percent: pilot 0%, scale 20%, enterprise 35%
- preemptable_discount_pct: 0.40 (40% cheaper when preemptable)

Illustrative outputs (rounded):
- pilot: effective_reserved_rate ~$1.80/hr, marginal_savings ~$1.70/hr at 60% util -> monthly savings vs on-demand ~$36k, months-to-amortize ~18 months
- scale: rate ~$1.20/hr, marginal_savings ~$2.30/hr at 78% util -> monthly savings ~$345k, months-to-amortize ~20 months
- enterprise: rate ~$0.75/hr, marginal_savings ~$2.75/hr at 92% util -> monthly savings ~$2.1M, months-to-amortize ~22 months

Why marginal cost matters for short commits:
- If a buyer wants a 6–12 month pilot, amortizing capex aggressively yields higher effective rates; decision should then be framed as "runway economics": what is the minimum utilization and revenue required to justify the pilot?
- Use marginal_savings_per_gpu_hour to show immediate unit-level gains even when amortization is unfavorable. This helps sales pitch shorter pilots that buy time-to-scale.

Sensitivity heatmap (structure):
- X axis: expected_utilization_percent (40%–100% in 5% steps)
- Y axis: preemptable_share_percent (0%–50% in 5% steps)
- Cell values: net_monthly_savings and months_to_amortize
- Color rules: red where net_monthly_savings < 0, amber where months_to_amortize > 30, green where net_monthly_savings > threshold and months_to_amortize <= 24

Tradeoffs and SLA implications:
- Higher preemptable_share reduces effective cost but increases probability of transient errors; recommend configurable "preemptable for non-critical inference jobs" contract clause and an SLO-aware tier (e.g., 99.5% latency SLA for non-preemptable; 98.0% for mixed pools).
- Provide a fallback buffer (5–10% of committed capacity) for enterprise buckets; finance can treat buffer as service-level reserve and price accordingly.

Three recommended commit templates (starting point for sales):
1) Pilot (3–6 months, small bucket): focus on quick time-to-value, limited amortization; on-premise-like SLA optional. Pricing: blended discount ~10–15%; require minimal preemptable (<=10%).
2) Scale (12–18 months, mid bucket): targeted for fast-growing customers who want predictable throughput. Blended discount 20–30%, allow 15–25% preemptable to lower unit cost, include step-up trigger at 6 months to re-evaluate utilization and add burst credits.
3) Enterprise (24–36 months, large bucket): deep discount (35–50%), allow 25–40% preemptable, include dedicated SLA and explicit buffer. Offer amortization-friendly invoicing (quarterly) and optional hardware affinity for privacy/regulatory customers.

Implementation notes for finance/ops: 
- Add a "runway" tab to the existing simulator that outputs months-to-amortize and per-token cost at different util/preemptable assumptions.
- Hook this to historical billing data (past 12 months) to seed expected_utilization_percent per-customer; use growth curves to project runway change over term.
- Build a simple API endpoint (internal) returning recommended commit_template given desired monthly capacity and preferred maximum preemptable_share.

Open questions / risks:
- Rate shapes: are we comfortable publishing preemptable discounts publicly (competitive leak)?
- Accounting: should we align amortization_months to hardware refresh cycles (some customers require 36 months)?
- Legal: what language around fallback and burst credits is acceptable for enterprise contracts?

Next steps / action items (owners assigned):
- Product (Aisha): produce final spreadsheet with heatmap, sample dashboard widgets, and commit templates (2 weeks).
- Finance (Noah): validate capex_equivalent_per_gpu and amortization policies and provide account-level historical utilization (1 week).
- Solutions (Liam): pilot with two interested customers, document SLA expectations and fallback behavior (4 weeks).

Quick links to run:
- Simulation notebook: github.com/redwood-inference/simulators/commit-runway (branch: runway-experiments)
- Confluence draft for legal: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/DEDICATED-LEGAL-CLAUSES

Notes to self (work-in-progress):
- We may want to surface a "utilization confidence" metric (95th percentile of weekly utilization) to reduce noisy month-to-month swings.
- Consider an optional "growth-escape clause" where a customer can add incremental capacity within first 6 months at guaranteed blended rates.

-- end of sheet --
